paras: The manhunt for the assailant of Florence Bruno and Annie Green was an armed search by hundreds of farmers, police and deputies east of East St. Louis, Illinois, begun on June 23, 1903, for an unidentified Black man accused of assaulting a white girl and a Black woman. Dispatches predicted he would be lynched or shot on sight, but no report shows the searchers seizing or harming anyone. Bruno died the next day; Green survived and later identified James Cross, who as James Northcross was sentenced to forty years for assaulting her.

The assaults took place on the afternoon of June 23 near Fireworks Station, between East St. Louis and Belleville in St. Clair County. Green, a Black woman aged 25, was clubbed and left with a fractured skull and broken arm, and before losing consciousness she described her attacker as "a light yellow negro" of about 25. Bruno, 17, her father's housekeeper, was found unconscious on her bed by her brother with her skull fractured and both arms broken.

A posse was summoned that afternoon, and by night the farmers, joined by the East St. Louis police chief and the St. Clair sheriff with deputies, had surrounded an unidentified man on an island formed by Mississippi floodwater. No later report says who he was or what became of him. The St. Louis Republic named the leaders as Sheriff Wash Thompson and Chief George O. Purdy and described "hundreds of farmers and citizens" armed with shotguns and revolvers. It reported that it was "openly stated" the farmers would shoot the man if they reached him first, while Thompson promised to swear in as many deputies as needed to protect a prisoner.

Bruno died at St. Mary's Hospital on the morning of June 24. Police arrested Black men in numbers ranging from six or fifteen in wire reports to more than 100 in the Republic, releasing them on alibis. Those held included Henry Griffin in St. Louis, William Wickes and Tom Moore at Flora, and Elija Shaw, alias John Smith, at Ashley.

A coroner's inquest found that Bruno died of a fractured skull at the hands of "a party or parties unknown." On June 25 detectives arrested James Cross near the scene of the Green assault, and Chief Purdy kept the arrest quiet, the Republic later said, for fear that friends of the Bruno family would try to seize him. Green failed to identify Cross positively in July but picked him from a Belleville line-up on October 22; he denied the charge and called it a "put-up job." In November a grand jury indicted James Northcross for assault with intent to murder Green, and on December 21 a Belleville jury sentenced him to forty years; he was never indicted for Bruno's death.

The first dispatch ran on June 24 from Indianapolis and Montgomery to Salt Lake City. Many headlines led with the expected lynching: "A Lynching in Prospect" in the Deseret Evening News, "Lynching Is Feared" in the Birmingham Age-Herald, and "Likely to Figure in Lynching Bee If Caught" in the Omaha Daily Bee. The Seattle Star called the man a "negro brute" who would be "lynched or shot down on the spot," and a Scripps-McRae telegram headed "Mob Will Avenge Girl's Murder" judged lynching prospects "good."

The St. Louis Republic, the only local paper in the coverage, followed the case into December, printing the threats alongside the sheriff's pledge and calling one suspect a "typical negro tramp." In the Black press the case appeared once, in the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate of June 25, which ran a shortened wire under "Mob After Another Negro" in a column of lynching reports. No Black paper in the coverage reported the arrests or the conviction.

The Seattle Star and the St. Landry Clarion placed the crime near St. Louis, while the local Republic and most wires placed it east of East St. Louis in Illinois. The accused appears as James Cross through October and as James Northcross in the indictment and sentencing, both times charged with the assault on Green. The Republic's October account said Green had identified him at the hospital soon after his arrest, but its July report said she had not.

reader.title: Manhunt for the assailant of Florence Bruno and Annie Green
bases: Armed farmers, police and deputies hunted a Black man accused of assaulting two women, with papers predicting a lynching or shooting on sight if he were caught (A1, A4, A13); no one is reported seized or harmed, so this is a threatened lynching.

Hundreds of armed searchers threatened to lynch or shoot the accused (A4, A13), but no report shows anyone killed or even seized by them; the accused James Cross/Northcross was held by police and tried (A24, A26).
The assaults, the armed hunt and the lynching threats are reported by the local St. Louis Republic and by separate wire and Scripps-McRae dispatches that agree on the core facts (A1, A13, A17).

accounts.label: June 23 St. Louis wire
accounts.gist: Two women, one white and one Black, assaulted and left for dead east of East St. Louis; a posse of farmers, police and deputies surrounded an unknown man on a flood island and a lynching was expected if he were caught.

accounts.label: Seattle Star dispatch
accounts.gist: Almost the entire St. Louis police force and several hundred suburban residents were hunting a 'negro brute' who would be 'lynched or shot down on the spot'.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republic (local)
accounts.gist: Sheriff Thompson and Chief Purdy led hundreds of armed farmers; over 100 Black men were arrested and released; it was openly said the farmers would shoot the man, while the sheriff pledged to protect a prisoner.

accounts.label: Scripps-McRae telegram
accounts.gist: Bruno died; six suspects under arrest; 'All prospects for a lynching are good.'

accounts.label: Black-press brief
accounts.gist: The wire, shortened, under 'Mob After Another Negro', saying both women would die.

accounts.label: Accused's statement
accounts.gist: Cross said he saw Green before the assault but did not commit it, was away at the time, never knew of Bruno, and called the line-up a 'put-up job'.

framing.detail: Wire papers ran the forecast lynching as the headline ('A Lynching in Prospect', 'Lynching Is Feared', 'Likely to Figure in Lynching Bee If Caught') without comment.
The Stark County Democrat's 'Mob Will Avenge Girl's Murder' called lynching prospects 'good', and the Grenada Sentinel wrote 'The brute remains uncaught'.
The local St. Louis Republic reported the threats, the sheriff's pledge and the court process, while calling one suspect a 'typical negro tramp'.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate reprinted the wire under 'Mob After Another Negro' in a column of lynching news.
